newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banacci, Bancomer results raise cheers in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Banacci, Bancomer results raise cheers in Mexico.

text.p: After months of keeping a wary distance, investors welcomed the first quarter results of Mexico's two biggest banks, and analysts said they may mark the start of a turnaround for downtrodden banking stocks.

Banacci, Mexico's largest banking group, posted a net gain of 971 million pesos, while its main rival Bancomer earned 349 million pesos. Both were big improvements on last year, but the comparisons were meaningless.

For the first time, the banks reported using U.S. accounting standards and analysts had awaited the results with trepidation, worried the new rules would reveal some nasty surprises that Mexico's old accounting standards concealed.

To their relief, no skeletons came tumbling out the closet. The amount of past-due loans was at least twice as much as it was under the previous rules, but the banks had predicted that in December. Interest earnings were unexpectedly positive.
"I believe the market and investors breathed a sigh of relief, and said, 'Hey, there are some earnings here'," said Brent Erensel, a banking analyst at UBS Securities in New York.

The good news occured in areas where the new accounting standards had been expected to deal their heaviest blows. The U.S. GAAP accounting makes the definition of delinquent loans more strict and curbs accrual of interest on non-performing loans, which had been expected to batter interest margins.
"The banks came in with two line items that were pleasing: Net interest margins, far from collapsing, actually held up and the level of past-due loans held fairly stable," Erensel said.
Stock prices of both banks surged on Friday after the reports, with Bancomer B shares climbing 6.95 percent to 2.77 pesos, and Banacci B shares up 3.41 percent to 16.98 pesos.
Erensel said the share performance could mark the start of a rally in bank stocks, which had been trampled in the first quarter as investors worried about the new GAAP standards.

"It's a classic banking recovery with a Mexican twist," he said. "I think the preponderance of the elements favor overweighting and invsting (in the banks), rather than bracing for the next bit of horrible news."
Susana Ornelas, banking analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, agreed Friday's rally was justified.

"At least some people were waiting to see first-quarter results (before buying)," she said. "Once they see past-due loans are stabilizing, the banks are creating reserves and doing charge-offs, it makes them feel a bit more comfortable."
In the case of Banacci's bank unit Banamex, the past-due loan ratio as a percentage of total loans was 20.5 percent while at Bancomer bank it was 19.2 percent.

Ornelas said Banamex's past-due mortgages increased more than she expected, rising by some three billion pesos, a turnaround from last quarter when it performed better in its mortgage portfolio than Bancomer.
On the other hand, she said Banacci's commercial past-due loans fell and the bank was more conservative than Bancomer in using tax credits to improve its appearance.

According to Carlos Gomez, bank analyst at Paribas in New York, Bancomer used some $250 million in deferred tax credits to boost assets, which sent shareholders equity soaring and may have helped explain why its shares rallied more than Banacci's on Friday.
However, Gomez praised Banacci "for using less smoke and mirrors", referring to its lower use of deferred tax credits.
